sourceBindings.text: A jar can help you see how prepared mineral soil separates in water. You will use a declared classroom procedure on three identified samples, mark the boundaries at the stated times and return to your own jars after the settling period. A prepared demonstration jar helps you practise reading, but it cannot prove you performed your own test.
Explain sand, silt and clay particle-size ranges, why a well-dispersed jar usually shows sand first and clay last, and why a classroom jar is not a standard laboratory texture determination.
Under trainer observation, prepare three identified samples with one declared jar, soil, water, dispersant, shaking and timing procedure while controlling container safety.

Return to each learner's own undisturbed jars, mark the actual boundaries at the procedure's scheduled stages and record uncertainty rather than inventing a line or using the trainer's prepared jar as personal evidence.

sourceBindings.text: A properly dispersed teaching jar has just been placed on a level bench. One learner labels the first basal layer clay because clay is 'heavy'.
In the stated size system sand grains are larger and generally settle sooner in this liquid system, creating the first visible mineral layer near the bottom.
Silt commonly follows and fine clay stays suspended longer; aggregates and different densities can disturb this simple sequence.
Record the actual visible sand boundary at the declared time instead of assuming a perfect line.
For the educational jar, sand first is the expected pattern, subject to method and observation.

sourceBindings.text: A trainee feels smooth flour and proposes putting it in the jar as the silt sample.
Flour can help describe a smooth or floury sensation, and silt may feel smooth and floury when dry or silky wet.
Flour is not mineral silt and may behave differently in water; use a labelled soil sample for the practical test.
A real field texture estimate uses the material's grain feel, behaviour when wet and an approved chart.
A tactile analogy is not an analytical substitute.

sourceBindings.text: A group shakes its jar, waits twenty minutes and reports exact sand, silt and clay percentages from its new sample.
The final clay boundary may need 24–48 hours in the selected classroom example; the short wait cannot establish the total mineral-layer height.
The group may record the early sand observation and use a labelled trainer-prepared jar to rehearse measurement.
They return to their own undisturbed jar later and complete its record only when the scheduled boundary is visible or state why it is not.
A prepared example teaches the skill but cannot replace each learner's later evidence.

Check the ID, actual shaking and dispersant record, then use safe side lighting without moving the jar.
Write that the interface is unclear and note the time and condition; do not copy a line or value from another sample.
Ask the trainer whether the selected procedure calls for a later observation or repeat, and document that decision.
Uncertainty is evidence to report, not a gap to hide.

sourceBindings.text: soil texture
The proportions by weight of sand-, silt- and clay-sized mineral particles in the <2 mm fine-earth fraction, or a qualified field estimate of the corresponding class.
sedimentation
Settling of suspended particles in a liquid under the selected conditions.
dispersant
A method-specified material used to separate soil aggregates so individual fine particles can settle more consistently.
sand
USDA mineral particle size about 0.05–2 mm.
silt
USDA mineral particle size about 0.002–0.05 mm.
clay
USDA mineral particle size below 0.002 mm.
loam
A USDA texture class covering a range of sand, silt and clay proportions, not a fourth particle or commercial potting medium.

The proportions by weight of sand-, silt- and clay-sized mineral particles in the <2 mm fine-earth fraction, or a qualified field estimate of the corresponding class.

sedimentation

Settling of suspended particles in a liquid under the selected conditions.

dispersant

A method-specified material used to separate soil aggregates so individual fine particles can settle more consistently.

sand

USDA mineral particle size about 0.05–2 mm.

silt

USDA mineral particle size about 0.002–0.05 mm.

clay

USDA mineral particle size below 0.002 mm.

loam

A USDA texture class covering a range of sand, silt and clay proportions, not a fourth particle or commercial potting medium.
